result: When I moved from Chicago to Denver, nobody warned me that altitude would humble me in the kitchen. I'd been baking sourdough casually for years at sea-level-ish elevation, so I assumed my starter, Gerald, would travel just fine. He did not. My first loaf came out dense as a paving stone, with a crust that could have doubled as a frisbee. The second overproofed in the dry mountain air and slumped into a sad, sprawling pancake. The third looked gorgeous going in, then collapsed the moment I scored it, and I may have said some things to the oven. I almost gave up and bought a loaf from the bakery down the street. Instead, I read up on high-altitude adjustments, cut my proofing time, bumped up the hydration, and started covering the dough more carefully. Loaf number four finally rose tall, with a crackly crust and an open, tender crumb. I stood in my kitchen, tearing off warm pieces, feeling like I'd finally arrived in Colorado. Gerald and I have a rhythm now, and the failures made that first slice taste even better.
